Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions
of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let
$T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Then the **Murphy basis
theorem** holds: the family
$$\mathcal M=\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$$
is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ is a cellular basis of $H$ in
the sense of [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]. Explicitly:
(i) $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all $\lambda$ and $s,t$; and (ii) for every
$\lambda$, every $t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ and every $h\in H$ there exist
$r_v\in R$ with
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}},$$
where $H^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the $m_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. The
theorem holds over every commutative coefficient ring with $q\in R^{\times}$
and assumes no semisimplicity; the total number of Murphy elements is
$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}|\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)|^2=n!$
([[cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers]]), matching the rank of $H$.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with
standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-automorphism $*$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a
composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put
$m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard
Young subgroup $S_\mu$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has
$|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional cellular algebra over a field $F$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) with cell modules
$C_\lambda$ and cell-form quotients $D_\lambda=C_\lambda/R_\lambda$. Then:

1. every nonzero $D_\lambda$ is an absolutely simple head, all simple
   $A$-modules occur exactly once this way, and $[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\ne0$ implies
   $\lambda\ge\mu$, with $[C_\mu:D_\mu]=1$ whenever $D_\mu\ne0$; here
   "nonzero quotient" means nonzero form, not necessarily a nondegenerate form
   on $C_\lambda$;
2. every nonzero cell module, including labels with zero-form quotient, has
   all its composition factors in a single block
   ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]);
3. two nonzero cell modules share a block exactly when they are linked by a
   finite chain of nonzero cell modules whose neighbouring terms share a
   simple composition factor;
4. for one primitive idempotent $e_\mu$ per simple,
   $$\dim_Fe_\mu Ae_\nu=\sum_\lambda[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\,[C_\lambda:D_\nu].$$

If the cellular index set $T(\lambda)$ is empty, then $C_\lambda=D_\lambda=0$.
Its block support, the set of primitive central idempotents $b$ with
$C_\lambda b\ne0$, is empty, and it has no simple composition factors.
It does not participate in the nonzero-cell linkage criterion of (3), and
its term in the corner sum of (4) is zero.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with its basis $\{m_t\}$, $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ and the DJ form on $P(\lambda)$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Then:

1. Setting $B_\lambda(m_s,p):=\beta(x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(s)},p)$ for $s\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ and $p\in P(\lambda)$ defines an explicit $R$-bilinear pairing $B_\lambda\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$ that is $H$-balanced, $B_\lambda(mh,p)=B_\lambda(m,ph^*)$, and whose adjoint $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$ is an isomorphism of right $H$-modules $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ onto the star-contragredient module of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. No nondegeneracy of the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ is required.

2. Equivalently, the kernel of the quotient map $M(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is the orthogonal complement $P(\lambda)^\perp=\{a\in M(\lambda):\beta(a,p)=0\text{ for all }p\in P(\lambda)\}$, namely $M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$; the pairing matrices in the bases $\{m_s\}$ and $\{e_t\}$ have entries $B_\lambda(m_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d_\lambda(s))}a_{d_\lambda(s),t}$ with $e_t=\sum_d a_{d,t}b_d$, and determinant a unit of $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. Their inverses are finite tableau formulas given by the adjugate divided by this unit.

3. All statements are compatible with every base change $A\to R$, $v\mapsto q$; the construction uses no generic semisimplicity, no nondegeneracy of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ and no choice principle.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: The row-double-coset identity and membership. For a semistandard tableau $S$ of shape $\lambda$ and type $\rho$ and a standard $t$ of shape $\lambda$, every row-standard refinement $s$ of the column-strict tableau $S$ is standard, and $\sum_sT_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda$ is the sum of $T_w$ over the double coset $S_\rho d(s_0)^{-1}S_\lambda$, each $w$ occurring exactly once; its left $S_\rho$-coset expansion writes it as $x_\rho h_0$, and appending $T_{d(t)}$ gives $m_{(S,t)}=x_\rho h$ for some $h\in H_n$. Hence each $m_{(S,t)}$ lies in $x_\rho H_n$, and no row-intersection quantum factorial is introduced.

Independence and the Garnir coefficient rules. The sums $m_{(S,t)}$ are $R$-independent because their Murphy fibres (the index sets $\{s:ho(s)=S\}$) are disjoint and every coefficient in the expansion of $m_{(S,t)}$ in the $m_{st}$ basis is $1$; they therefore have disjoint unit pivots. For the coefficient rules, consider a violation at adjacent rows $i,i+1$ and column $j$ and the composition $
u=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{i-1},j-1,\lambda_i+1,\lambda_{i+1}-j,\lambda_{i+2},\dots)$; the two length-additive coset sums of $S_
u S_\lambda$ give $\sum_{w\in S_
u\cap D_\lambda}x_\lambda T_w =\sum_{v\in S_\lambda\cap D_
u}T_v^*x_
u,$ whose distinguished Garnir term occurs with coefficient $1$. Every other term in the original shape has strictly more dominant row tableaux, the reordered $
u$ has strictly higher lexicographic shape, and the ordinary Murphy dominance refinement places these shape errors in higher-cell ideals; a nonstandard tableau factors as that Garnir tableau followed by an additive-length word (removing inversions while keeping the column violation), and Bruhat subword support preserves the strict tableau-prefix inequality. In the isolated relation for consecutive $a,a+1$ in one column, sorting the Garnir belt has a unique standard term whose single adjacent swap produces the distinguished Garnir term, with coefficient $-1$, and every other same-shape term is strictly more dominant. This yields the displayed congruence of the Statement, and the right analogue follows by the cellular involutions $*$.

The row eigenspace test. For a fixed $a$ the left $z$-eigenspace of $T_a$ in $H_n$ is $(1+T_a)H_n$: in the $T_w$ basis pair $w$ with $s_aw$ of larger length, and coefficient comparison in $T_ah=zh$ gives equality of the two coefficients, whose sum is $(1+T_a)T_w$. This argument uses only that $z$ is a unit. Over the universal domain, no element of this space has a nonzero Murphy coefficient at a tableau with $a,a+1$ in one column: choose a least shape and then a least left tableau in a dominance-compatible support order; higher-cell terms cannot contribute to its shape, and a column correction from another tableau can contribute only from a strictly less dominant left tableau, absent by minimality. If $a,a+1$ are in a column, its coefficient in $T_ah$ is the negative of its coefficient in $h$ by step 1.2, contradicting the eigenvalue equation since $z+1\ne0$ in the domain; if they share a row, the basis element is already a $z$-eigenvector and is subtracted; if their swap is standard, the exact two-tableau rules make the two coefficients equal and their sum is a $z$-eigenvector, which is subtracted. Each subtraction stays in the row ideal and removes the chosen support term without creating new ones, so induction on the finite support proves the column exclusion; specializing the resulting coordinate-zero identities gives it over every base ring, with no division by $z+1$ at a singular parameter.

The basis theorem. Let $h\in x_\rho H_n$. It is a $z$-eigenvector for every generator inside every $\rho$-row interval, so step 2.1 excludes any supported tableau with a consecutive pair inside one column; for an adjacent standard swap, comparison of the exact two-tableau equations makes the two coefficients equal (no column-state correction can interfere, since every such state has coefficient $0$). The standard refinements of a fixed row-label tableau are the linear extensions of the finite node posets of its repeated-label classes, and any two are connected by swaps of adjacent incomparable elements; finite induction on the inversion distance shows that if a repeated label occupies one column, a consecutive vertical cover realises an excluded state and forces the whole fibre coefficient to be $0$, while otherwise the row-label tableau is column-strict and every fibre coefficient equals one common value. Hence $h$ has zero coefficients off semistandard fibres and constant coefficients on each semistandard fibre, i.e. $h$ lies in the span of the $m_{(S,t)}$; with step 1.2 this proves that the $m_{(S,t)}$ form an $R$-basis of $x_\rho H_n$.

The two filtrations, keeping the ordinary dictionary explicit. The higher-shape Murphy-cell filtration obtained from [F1] has one quotient $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ for every semistandard tableau $S$ of shape $\lambda$ and type $\rho$: its second-index action is the fixed-first-index Murphy cell action. These quotients are free over $R$, so every short exact sequence of this filtration splits as a sequence of $R$-modules. Star duality is therefore exact on this filtration. On the distinguished coset basis $b_d=x_\rho T_d$ of $x_\rho H_n$, define $\beta(b_d,b_c)=\delta_{dc}z^{\ell(d)}$. The row-permutation generator cases prove contravariance: a same-row generator acts by $z$; a length-increasing adjacent coset pair acts by $b_dT_i=b_c$, $b_cT_i=z b_d+(z-1)b_c$, with $\ell(c)=\ell(d)+1$, and the diagonal weights give $\beta(b_dT_i,b_c)=z^{\ell(c)}=z\beta(b_d,b_d)$. All other entries are zero or the corresponding diagonal equality. Thus $\beta$ gives an $H_n$-isomorphism $x_\rho H_n\cong(x_\rho H_n)^\circ$, since every diagonal $z^{\ell(d)}$ is a unit. The independently proved same-shape bridge gives $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\circ\cong P(\lambda)$, the ordinary Dipper–James Specht module, by finite-free biduality. Dualize the split Murphy filtration and transport it through this permutation self-duality. The resulting reversed filtration is an ordinary Specht filtration with exactly the same multiplicities. The original Murphy filtration is not called the ordinary one. This preserves the full every-ring/unit-parameter existence Statement without generic semisimplicity or form nondegeneracy on a Specht module.

The generic multiplicity interpretation. Over the generic field the finite Hecke algebra is split semisimple: by [F2] every simple is a nonzero cellular head, a simple factor of an ordinary cell module has a word character from that module and from the head's own cell shape, and disjoint word sets force the shapes to agree; existence of a factor forces its own head to be nonzero, diagonal multiplicity $1$ forces the cell module to be simple, and the sum of squared dimensions equals the Hecke rank, so the algebra and each parabolic are split semisimple. Consequently the filtration multiplicity $\#\operatorname{SStd}_\rho(\lambda)$ equals the multiplicity of the trivial character of the $\rho$-row parabolic in $S^\lambda$, by induction/restriction adjunction in the semisimple category.

Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1 prove the semistandard Murphy basis of $x_\rho H_n$, step 1.2 gives the explicit Garnir and same-column generator rules with their termination, step 4.1 gives the Specht filtration with multiplicity $\#\operatorname{SStd}_\rho(\lambda)$, and step 5.1 gives the generic parabolic-multiplicity interpretation. Everything is proved universally over $\mathbb Z[z,z^{-1}]$ and specializes; the row-double-coset membership uses each coset word once and introduces no quantum-factorial division.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let $L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]).

derivations.claim: Surjectivity of the natural map. By [F1] the first polynomial generator is the scalar $q^j$ (respectively $j$), and the recursion expressing every $X_{r+1}$ (respectively $x_{r+1}$) in $X_r$ and $T_r$ (respectively $s_r$) shows that the algebra generated by the finite generators and $X_1$ is already generated by the finite generators alone. Hence the assignment of the Statement is a surjective algebra homomorphism. [F1, algebra]

The inverse in the nondegenerate branch. Let $L_r$ be the additive Jucys–Murphy element and put $M_r:=1+(q-1)L_r=q^{1-r}T_{r-1}\cdots T_1^{\,2}\cdots T_{r-1},$ a product of units, so every $M_r$ is invertible; the $M_r$ commute because the $L_r$ do, and $T_rM_rT_r=qM_{r+1}$ while $T_rM_t=M_tT_r$ for $t\notin\{r,r+1\}$ follow from [F2] by separating the term $a=r$ in $L_{r+1}$ and using the finite braid relation on the three affected transpositions. Setting $X_r:=q^jM_r$ therefore produces commuting units with $T_rX_rT_r=qX_{r+1}$, distant mixed commutation, the finite Hecke relations and $X_1=q^j$. These elements satisfy the complete affine presentation, so the assignment defines a homomorphism $H^\Lambda_d\to H_{F,q}(S_d)$ fixing the $T_r$. [F1, F2, construct]

The inverse in the degenerate branch. Put $x_r:=j+L_r$ with $L_r=\sum_{a<r}(a\ r)\in FS_d$. Direct transposition multiplication gives $s_rL_{r+1}s_r=L_r+s_r$, hence $s_rx_{r+1}=x_rs_r+1$, and the $x_r$ commute and commute with distant generators by [F2]; at $r=1$ this gives $x_1=j$. These elements satisfy the degenerate affine relations, so the assignment defines a homomorphism $H^\Lambda_d\to FS_d$ fixing the $s_r$. [F1, F2, construct]

Mutual inverses. The two constructions of steps 1.2 and 1.3 fix every finite generator, and the composites with the surjection of step 1.1 fix every presentation generator: the finite generators by construction, and the polynomial generators because both sides satisfy the same recursion from $X_1=q^j$ (respectively $x_1=j$) and the mixed relations. Hence both composites are the identity on a generating set, so the maps are mutually inverse isomorphisms; rank zero gives $F$ on both sides. This removes any late-basis or dimension dependency and introduces no BK or primitive-block input. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations $(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with $T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): 1.

Let $R=\mathbb Z[z^{\pm1},U_1^{\pm1},\dots,U_\ell^{\pm1}]$ with $\ell\ge1$, and let $H_n$ be the actual nondegenerate cyclotomic presentation of [[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]] at the first polynomial $\prod_a(X_1-U_a)$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is $$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$ The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.
For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring, $$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

derivations.claim: The trace and its dual basis. Define $\tau\colon H_n\to R$ by $\tau(\mathcal B)=1$ at the zero-dot identity word and $0$ at every other PBW basis element, extended $R$-linearly; by [F1] this is well defined over $R$ and after base change. Put $J_1=1$ and $J_i=q_H^{-1}T_{i-1}J_{i-1}T_{i-1}$ in the finite Hecke subalgebra; the $J_i$ are units. Define the second family $\mathcal C=\bigl\{T_vJ_1^{\delta(c_1)}\cdots J_n^{\delta(c_n)} X_1^{c_1}\cdots X_n^{c_n}:0\le c_i<\ell,\ v\in S_n\bigr\},\qquad \delta(0)=0,\ \delta(c)=-1\ (c>0).$ The standard anti-involution fixing the presentation generators fixes each $X_i$, so $\mathcal B^*=\{T_vX^c\}$ is a basis; at each fixed profile $c$, multiplying the finite Hecke factor by the unit $J_1^{\delta(c_1)}\cdots J_n^{\delta(c_n)}$ is an invertible $R$-linear change of the finite Hecke basis. Hence $\mathcal C$ is an $R$-basis of $H_n$. [F1, construct]

Cyclicity for $X_1$ via the tower. At rank one the algebra is commutative, so cyclicity is immediate; for the induction assume $n\ge2$. Identify $H_{n-1}$ with the subalgebra on $X_1,\dots,X_{n-1},T_1,\dots,T_{n-2}$; its bounded words are a subset of $\mathcal B$. Put $v_k=s_{n-1}\cdots s_k$ for $1\le k<n$ and $v_n=1$; the decomposition $w=uv_k$ with $u\in S_{n-1}$ is length additive, so $\{X_n^aT_{v_k}:0\le a<\ell,\ 1\le k\le n\}$ is a left $H_{n-1}$-basis of $H_n$. Define the left-linear projection $E_n\colon H_n\to H_{n-1}$ to be $1$ on $X_n^0T_{v_n}$ and $0$ on the other basis elements, and $\tau_n=\tau_{n-1}\circ E_n$. With $V=T_{n-1}\cdots T_1$ and $U=(T_{n-1}-q_H+1)\cdots(T_1-q_H+1)$, the mixed relation gives $VX_1=X_nU$, and [F2] gives $VX_1^m=X_n^mU+J_m$, where every term of $J_m$ has total dot degree $m$ and $X_n$-degree between $1$ and $m-1$ (the leading branch transfers the full exponent, each correction transfers a strictly smaller positive exponent, and no variable above $n$ occurs). For $m\le\ell$ every lower exponent in $J_m$ is below $\ell$, so $E_n(J_m)=0$; likewise $E_n(X_n^mU)=0$ for $1\le m<\ell$. Multiplying the first-dot relation $f(X_1)=0$ by $V$ gives $0=X_n^\ell U+J_\ell+\sum_{m=1}^{\ell-1}c_m(X_n^mU+J_m)+c_0V$, and applying $E_n$ yields $E_n(X_n^\ell U)=0$, which completes the missing case $m=\ell$. To verify right $X_1$-linearity, test the displayed left tower basis $X_n^aT_{v_k}$. For $k\ge2$, $T_{v_k}$ and $X_n$ commute with $X_1$; its projection is zero unless $a=0,k=n$, where the equality is immediate. For $k=1$, $VX_1=X_nU$ gives $E_n(X_n^aVX_1)=E_n(X_n^{a+1}U)=0$ for $0\le a<\ell$: bounded positive exponents project to zero, and the endpoint $a+1=\ell$ was just established. Left $H_{n-1}$-linearity then extends the equality to every $h$. Hence $E_n(hX_1)=E_n(h)X_1$ for all $h$, and by left linearity $E_n(X_1h)=X_1E_n(h)$; induction on $n$ gives $\tau_n(X_1h)=\tau_n(hX_1)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

Cyclicity for the finite generators. Let $p=X^a$ be a bounded dot monomial and $w\in S_n$. By [F2], $T_jp=(s_jp)T_j+(1-q_H)X_{j+1}\frac{p-s_jp}{X_j-X_{j+1}};$ for $p=X_j^aX_{j+1}^b$ times the other variables, the correction monomials have the same total dot degree and both displayed exponents at most $\max(a,b)<\ell$ (the exponents run as $(a-1-k,b+1+k)$ or $(a+k,b-k)$), so when the exponent profile is positive every term on either side of $\tau(T_jpT_w)=\tau(pT_wT_j)$ has a positive bounded profile and evaluates to $0$. When $p=1$, the finite Hecke multiplication formula [F1] gives coefficient of $1$ in $T_jT_w$, respectively $T_wT_j$, equal to $q_H$ if $w=s_j$ and $0$ otherwise. This proves $\tau(T_jh)=\tau(hT_j)$ without using the trace one is proving. [F1, F2, algebra]

Generation and symmetry. The elements $X_1,T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ generate $H_n$ as an $R$-algebra: the constant term $c_0=(-1)^\ell\prod_aQ_a$ is a unit, so $f(X_1)=0$ makes $X_1^{-1}$ a polynomial in $X_1$; each $T_j^{-1}=q_H^{-1}(T_j-q_H+1)$; and $X_r=q_H^{1-r}T_{r-1}\cdots T_1X_1T_1\cdots T_{r-1}$, with inverses expressed likewise. Moving the generators of a word one at a time around $\tau$, using steps 1.2 and 1.3, gives $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ for every pair of words, hence for all $a,b$ by $R$-bilinearity; the pairing $(a,b)\mapsto\tau(ab)$ is associative and symmetric. [step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

Perfectness. Let $G_j$ be the matrix of the pairing between $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ restricted to profiles whose entries above $j$ vanish (all finite permutations included), of size $N_j=\ell^jn!$; order the new last profiles by $b_{j+1}=0,1,\dots,\ell-1$ and $c_{j+1}=0,\ell-1,\ell-2,\dots,1$. Cyclicity rotates the rightmost dot monomial to the front, combining exponents; if both new exponents are $0$ the block is $G_j$; if $0<b+c<\ell$ it is zero by step 1.2; if $b+c=\ell$ the cyclotomic reduction of the first variable applies: with $\alpha=(-1)^{\ell+1}Q_1\cdots Q_\ell$ one obtains $\tau(X_{j+1}^\ell h)=\alpha\,\tau(hJ_{j+1})$ (the right factor $J_{j+1}^{-1}$ occurring in $\mathcal C$ cancels the $J_{j+1}$), so the block is $\alpha G_j$. After the stated column permutation $G_{j+1}$ is block lower triangular with one diagonal block $G_j$ and $\ell-1$ diagonal blocks $\alpha G_j$; by [F3], $\det G_{j+1}=\pm\,\alpha^{(\ell-1)N_j}(\det G_j)^\ell .$ The base matrix $G_0=(\tau(T_wT_v))$ has entries $q_H^{\ell(w)}\delta_{v,w^{-1}}$ by the finite Hecke multiplication rule [F1], so its determinant is a unit. Induction makes $\det G_n$ a unit; equivalently, the bases $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ pair unimodularly, so $\tau$ identifies $H_n$ with its $R$-dual and the pairing is perfect over $R$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Base change and boundary cases. Presentation base change commutes with forming $H_n$, and the universal PBW basis is free, so the trace coefficients and the inverse Gram matrix base-change to any commutative ring in which all parameters remain units; in particular they do so for the LM deformation DVR with $q_Ht$ and $Q_at^{na}$. For $n=0$ use $H_0=R$ with $\tau(1)=1_R$; for $\ell=1$ the family $\mathcal C$ consists of finite $T_v$ and the same proof applies. The separate level-zero positive-rank quotient is $0$, with the zero perfect pairing, and no claim $\tau(1)=1$ is made for it. No generic faithfulness or imported Bremke–Malle trace statement is used. [step 1.1, step 2.2] ∎

citations.quote: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations $(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with $T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): 1.

For $n\ge2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ has the presentation $$S_n=\langle s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\mid s_i^2=1,\ s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1},\ s_is_j=s_js_i\ (|i-j|>1)\rangle,$$ where, after relabelling the underlying set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ as $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $s_i$ corresponds to the adjacent transposition $(i\ i+1)$.

For every commutative ring $R$ with invertible parameter $z$, the ordinary finite type-A Hecke algebra $H_n$ and a composition $\rho$ of $n$, the permutation module $x_\rho H_n$ has $R$-basis $$m_{(S,t)}=\sum_{s:\,\rho(s)=S}m_{st},$$ where $S$ ranges over the semistandard tableaux of partition shape and type $\rho$ and $t$ over the standard tableaux of the same shape.
For every $n\ge0$, $$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2=n!,$$ where $f^\lambda$ is the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux and $f^\varnothing=1$, $0!=1$.

derivations.claim: Finite-generator straightening. Every component-preserving row-standard multitableau factors its distinguished permutation into a permutation inside the contiguous component intervals followed by the unique shuffle of the intervals preserving internal order; the two inversion sets are disjoint, so the factorization is length-additive. Multiplying by $u_\lambda$ (which commutes with the Hecke generators internal to the intervals), ordinary Murphy straightening applies in each component; higher ordinary component shapes preserve component sizes and strictly increase multipartition dominance, and the final component shuffle relabels each component by an increasing list whose selected entries at any cutoff are an initial segment, so tableau-prefix inequalities are exactly the ordinary ones at the corresponding initial-segment length. For a fixed initial left row and right multiplication by $T_i$: if $ts_i$ is standard the length formula gives the usual standard term (or $q_H$ times it plus $(q_H-1)m_{t^\lambda t}$); if $i,i+1$ share a row the result is $q_Hm$; and if they share a component but the interchange fails standardness, factoring out the increasing component shuffle and applying the ordinary cell law gives same-shape terms with the same initial left row and strictly higher multipartition terms, the required transfer identity $T_cT_i=T_jT_c$ following from $cs_i=s_jc$ and the length/quadratic formula. A cross-component column failure is impossible because column standardness is imposed componentwise. Descending induction over a linear extension of multipartition dominance therefore makes each $N^{\ge\lambda}$ and $N^{>\lambda}$ stable under all finite generators; multiplying on the left by $T_{d(s)}^*$ and applying $*$ makes the higher spans two-sided ideals. This induction concerns spanning sets only and assumes no independence. [F1, algebra]

The cyclotomic component shift. Let $a=(a_k)$ with $a_k=\sum_{b<k}|\lambda^{(b)}|$ and $u_a=u_\lambda$, and let $b=a+e_k$. Put $u_b=u_a(X_{a_k+1}-Q_k)$; the factors commute, and for $a=a_k$ the defining recurrence gives the exact identity $u_aT_a\cdots T_1X_1T_1\cdots T_a=q_H^a igl(Q_ku_a+u_b igr),$ by substituting $T_a\cdots T_1X_1T_1\cdots T_a=q_H^aX_{a+1}$ and adding/subtracting $Q_ku_a$; the case $a=0$ is included. For $k>1$ form the multicomposition $
u$ obtained by appending a singleton row to component $k-1$ and deleting the first node of the first row of component $k$. Its cumulative sizes are $b$, so $u_
u=u_b$, and its Young subgroup is contained in $S_\lambda$; the left length-additive coset expansion gives $x_\lambda u_b=\sum_vT_v^*m_
u$. Sorting the rows of $
u$ in each component conjugates its Young subgroup and gives $m_
u=T_dm_{\operatorname{sort}
u}T_d^{-1}$ with $u_
u$ commuting with the component-preserving permutation, so the ordinary row-sorting argument expresses each term in standard pairs of shapes at least $\operatorname{sort}
u$, which strictly dominates $\lambda$: the cumulative total through component $k-1$ strictly increases and no later cumulative sum decreases. Hence $x_\lambda u_b\in N^{>\lambda}$. For $k=1$, nonemptiness of component $1$ forces $a_s\ge1$ for all $s\ge2$, so $u_b$ contains every factor $(X_1-Q_s)$ and vanishes by the cyclotomic relation; again $x_\lambda u_b\in N^{>\lambda}$. [F1, algebra]

Right multiplication by $X_1$. Let $t$ be standard with entry $1$ in component $k$, an initial node, and initial label $a+1$ with $a=a_k$. Then $d(t)=(s_a\cdots s_1)w$ with $w$ fixing $1$ and $\ell(d(t))=a+\ell(w)$: pulling label $a+1$ to value $1$ crosses exactly the $a$ smaller initial labels, whose final values exceed $1$. A permutation fixing $1$ has a reduced word in $s_2,\dots,s_{n-1}$, so $T_w$ commutes with $X_1$. Multiplying the identity of step 1.2 on the right by $(T_1\cdots T_a)^{-1}$ and then by $T_w$ gives $m_\lambda T_{d(t)}X_1=q_H^aQ_km_\lambda(T_1\cdots T_a)^{-1}T_w +q_H^ax_\lambda u_b(T_1\cdots T_a)^{-1}T_w,$ whose second term lies in $N^{>\lambda}$ by step 1.2 and finite-generator stability, and whose first term lies modulo $N^{>\lambda}$ in the fixed-initial-row span. Hence that span is stable under $X_1$; multiplying on the left by $T_{d(s)}^*$ and using the left stability of the higher shapes gives the coefficient-independence law $m_{st}h\equiv\sum_vr_{(t,v)}(h)m_{sv}\pmod{N^{>\lambda}}$ first for each generator and then for every word, with coefficients independent of $s$, and $*$ makes the higher spans two-sided. Since $X_r=q_H^{1-r}T_{r-1}\cdots T_1X_1T_1\cdots T_{r-1}$ and the cyclotomic constant term is a unit when the $Q_a$ are invertible, these generators generate the Laurent affine quotient. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Spanning and cellularity. The smallest multipartition $\omega=(\varnothing,\dots,\varnothing,(1^n))$ satisfies $u_\omega=x_\omega=m_\omega=1$, so the generator-stable span of the standard $m_{st}$ contains $1$ and is all of $H_n$: the Murphy family spans. By [[lem-universal-cyclotomic-hecke-ordered-monomials-form-a-basis]], $H_n$ is independently free of rank $\ell^nn!$. Counting standard pairs with the ordinary identity $\sum_{\rho\vdash m}f_\rho^2=m!$ at the component sizes $n_a$ contributes $(n!)^2/\prod_an_a!$, and summing over the multipartition compositions gives $\ell^nn!$ by the multinomial theorem. The spanning family therefore has exactly the independent rank; its coefficient matrix in the ordered PBW basis is square and surjective between free modules, hence invertible, so the family is an $R$-basis and the proved involution and coefficient-independence laws are actual cellularity. Tensoring the proved basis and presentation supplies every commutative specialization with unit parameters, including repeated charges and the LM deformation DVR; no generic-flatness inference is made. Rank zero is the singleton empty basis. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Conclusion. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 establish the generator-stable higher ideals for the finite-generator subalgebra; step 2.1 extends stability to $X_1$ and hence to all polynomial generators and gives the coefficient-independence law with two-sided higher spans; and step 3.1 proves that the standard Murphy family is an $R$-basis of exactly the independent rank, so that the involution and coefficient laws are cellularity in the sense of the Definition. Every commutative specialization with unit parameters inherits the basis and the cell law. No primitive-block classification is used. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge0$ and $\ell\ge1$, and let $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$
be units of $R$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). The **arbitrary-level
cyclotomic Hecke algebra** $H_n=H_n(R;z;U_1,\dots,U_\ell)$ is the $R$-algebra
presented by invertible commuting elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ subject to the relations
$$(T_i-z)(T_i+1)=0,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$
$$T_iX_iT_i=zX_{i+1},\qquad X_jT_i=T_iX_j\quad(j\notin\{i,i+1\}),\qquad \prod_{a=1}^{\ell}(X_1-U_a)=0 .$$
For $n=0$ set $H_0=R$. The **grading variable** of this page is $v$, not the
unit $z$: the two are identified only where a statement says so explicitly.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

derivations.claim: Initial-row eigenvalues. For component $k$ and $a=a_k$, [F1] gives $m_\lambda(X_{a+1}-Q_k)=x_\lambda u_b\in N^{>\lambda}$. The internal finite Hecke submodule generated by $m_\lambda$ modulo higher global shapes is spanned by standard internal component permutations; each such permutation fixes the smallest internal label $a+1$ (that label occupies the first node of its component), so its Hecke element has a reduced word in the internal generators with indices at least $a+2$ and commutes with $X_{a+1}$. Hence $X_{a+1}$ acts as the scalar $Q_k$ on that whole submodule, with errors in the two-sided ideal $N^{>\lambda}$. The $X$-recurrence then identifies $X_{a+i}$ on this submodule with $Q_k$ times the ordinary multiplicative Jucys–Murphy element $M_i$ of [F2], by induction from the finite quadratic relation and the additive-JM recurrence (a polynomial identity also at $q_H=1$). Ordinary JM triangularity gives diagonal $Q_kq_H^{c-r}$ at the node $(r,c,k)$ occupied by local entry $i$: the internal label $i$ is not a row index, and no extra subtraction of $i-1$ occurs. For the initial component tableau, which is maximal in tableau dominance, there are no strictly more dominant same-shape terms. Thus for the node $(r,c,k)$ carrying global entry $t$, $m_\lambda X_t\equiv Q_kq_H^{c-r}m_\lambda\pmod{N^{>\lambda}}$.

JM triangularity for every standard multitableau. Inducting through a reduced word of $w$, the relations [F1] give $T_wX_r=X_{w(r)}T_w+\sum_{v<w}\sum_ba_{(v,b)}X_bT_v,$ where the corrections are supported on proper Bruhat subwords (at the first correction a generator is deleted, moving its linear $X$-coefficient through preceding generators deletes further generators, and finite quadratic multiplication preserves Bruhat support). Applying this with $w=d(t)$ and multiplying by $m_\lambda$ on the left, step 1.1 evaluates every surviving $X$ coefficient modulo higher shapes; a correction $m_\lambda T_v$ reduces first to a row-standard representative $d(u)$ of its Young-subgroup coset, the removed row subgroup contributing its row eigenvalue, with $d(u)\le v<d(t)$; the Bruhat/tableau-prefix relation on the ordered rows of all components then makes $u$ strictly dominate $t$, and componentwise straightening of $u$ keeps the shape or produces same-shape tableaux at least $u$ in prefix dominance, hence strictly dominating $t$. The leading eigenvalue is $Q_kq_H^{j-i}$ at the node carrying $r$, because $w(r)$ is its initial-row label under $t=t^\lambda\cdot w=w^{-1}\cdot t^\lambda$. Therefore $m_{(t^\lambda,t)}X_r\equiv Q_kq_H^{j-i}m_{(t^\lambda,t)} +\sum_{v\lhd t}a_vm_{(t^\lambda,v)}\pmod{N^{>\lambda}},$ the exact arbitrary-level JM content statement, independent of an affine center theorem, semisimplicity or block classification. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

Residue words and boundary cases. On the resulting Specht module a total ordering extending tableau dominance triangularizes all the $X_r$ simultaneously; the one-dimensional successive quotients have exactly the content characters of step 2.1, so every simultaneous generalized eigenword is among the standard-tableau residue words $c_a+j-i\pmod e$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]] for the ordinary part); the residue multiplicities of every such word equal the node-residue multiplicities of $\lambda$, since permuting the labels of a standard tableau does not change the multiset of node residues. For rank zero, $H=F$, the sole shape and tableau are empty and all assertions have their one-dimensional interpretation. The triangularity is polynomial in the parameters, so it specializes to the LM deformation DVR and to the generic fibre.

For $H_n$ in [[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]] over the universal Laurent parameter ring, the elements $m_{st}$ indexed by all $\ell$-multipartitions of $n$ and standard tableaux $s,t$ of that shape are a basis and a dominance-cellular datum: $$m_{st}^*=m_{ts},\qquad m_{st}h\equiv\sum_vr_{(t,v)}(h)\,m_{sv}\pmod{H^{>\lambda}},$$ with coefficients $r_{(t,v)}(h)$

For every commutative ring $R$ with invertible parameter $z$, the ordinary finite type-A Hecke algebra $H_n$ and a composition $\rho$ of $n$, the permutation module $x_\rho H_n$ has $R$-basis $$m_{(S,t)}=\sum_{s:\,\rho(s)=S}m_{st},$$ where $S$ ranges over the semistandard tableaux of partition shape and type $\rho$ and $t$ over the standard tableaux of the same shape.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations $(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with $T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): 1.

For $n\ge2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ has the presentation $$S_n=\langle s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\mid s_i^2=1,\ s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1},\ s_is_j=s_js_i\ (|i-j|>1)\rangle,$$ where, after relabelling the underlying set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ as $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $s_i$ corresponds to the adjacent transposition $(i\ i+1)$.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional cellular algebra over a field $F$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) with cell modules
$C_\lambda$ and cell-form quotients $D_\lambda=C_\lambda/R_\lambda$. Then:

1. every nonzero $D_\lambda$ is an absolutely simple head, all simple
   $A$-modules occur exactly once this way, and $[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\ne0$ implies
   $\lambda\ge\mu$, with $[C_\mu:D_\mu]=1$ whenever $D_\mu\ne0$; here
   "nonzero quotient" means nonzero form, not necessarily a nondegenerate form
   on $C_\lambda$;
2. every nonzero cell module, including labels with zero-form quotient, has
   all its composition factors in a single block
   ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]);
3. two nonzero cell modules share a block exactly when they are linked by a
   finite chain of nonzero cell modules whose neighbouring terms share a
   simple composition factor;
4. for one primitive idempotent $e_\mu$ per simple,
   $$\dim_Fe_\mu Ae_\nu=\sum_\lambda[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\,[C_\lambda:D_\nu].$$

If the cellular index set $T(\lambda)$ is empty, then $C_\lambda=D_\lambda=0$.
Its block support, the set of primitive central idempotents $b$ with
$C_\lambda b\ne0$, is empty, and it has no simple composition factors.
It does not participate in the nonzero-cell linkage criterion of (3), and
its term in the corner sum of (4) is zero.

On the Specht module $S_\lambda$ of [[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]], $X_r$ acts dominance-triangularly with diagonal $U_az^{j-i}$ at the node $(i,j,a)$ carrying $r$.

derivations.claim: The affine expansion with only variable-difference denominators. Writing $T_w$ as the product of the $\Phi_i$ and the scalars $c_{i,i+1}$ along a reduced word of $w$ and moving a Laurent polynomial $f$ leftward across the $\Phi$'s by [F2] expresses $T_wf$ as a sum of terms $c_v\,v(f)$ times a monomial in a subword, where $v$ runs over products of subwords of that reduced word, every denominator of $c_v$ is a product of differences $X_i-X_j$, and each $v$ is Bruhat-below $w$ by the subword characterization of Bruhat order ([F6]). In particular applying this with $f=u_\lambda$ keeps all denominators among the variable differences and introduces no $U_a-U_b$, quantum factorial, or Gram determinant. [F1, F2, F6, algebra]

Flagging is Bruhat-downward closed and gives monic divisibility. Let $S$ be semistandard of shape $\lambda$ and type $\mu$, and for a permutation $\sigma$ let $\pi=\sigma^{-1}$ map each label to its physical position; set $A_k=\sum_{a<k}|\lambda^{(a)}|$ and $B_k=\sum_{a<k}|\mu^{(a)}|$. By [F1] the flag condition says that a label of component $a$ occupies only a physical component $b\le a$, i.e. $\#\{r\le B_k:\pi(r)\le A_k\}=B_k$ for all $k$. The count is at most $B_k$; inversion preserves the Bruhat order and a Bruhat-smaller permutation has at least as many entries in every prefix rectangle, so every Bruhat-smaller permutation of a flagged one is flagged. If $\sigma$ is flagged then $\sigma(u_\lambda)=\prod_k\prod_{j\le A_k}(X_{\sigma(j)}-U_k)$ contains the factor $(X_r-U_k)$ for every $r\le B_k$, because $\pi(r)\le A_k$; hence $\sigma(u_\lambda)=u_\mu\prod_j\prod_{a(j)<k\le b(j)}(X_j-U_k)$ with $a(j)$ the physical component of the position occupied by label $j$ and $b(j)$ its type component, a monic polynomial. In particular $u_\mu$ divides $\sigma(u_\lambda)$ in the Laurent polynomial ring. [F1, F6, algebra]

The left row-double-coset identity and localized membership. Let $s_0$ be the least standard refinement of $S$ and $D=S_\mu d(s_0)^{-1}S_\lambda$. Every row-standard refinement of the semistandard $S$ is standard, and the ordinary length-additive left row-double-coset expansion gives $\sum_{s:\,\mu(s)=S}T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda=\sum_{w\in D}T_w$, each element of $D$ exactly once, with no row-intersection quantum factorial ([F4] proves the identical finite identity; [F1] fixes the elements $T_{d(s)}^*$ and $x_\lambda$). Since $S_\mu$ permutes labels inside $\mu$-components and $S_\lambda$ permutes positions inside $\lambda$-rows, every $w\in D$ is flagged; hence every Bruhat-subword permutation $v$ in the expansion of step 1.1 is flagged by step 1.2, so $v(u_\lambda)=u_\mu g_v$ with $g_v$ a Laurent polynomial, and $T_wu_\lambda\in u_\mu H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}[(X_i-X_j)^{-1}]$ for every $w\in D$. Writing $b_0:=\sum_{w\in D}T_w$ and summing, $b_0u_\lambda\in u_\mu H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}[(X_i-X_j)^{-1}]$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

The flagged span is a right ideal and a left parabolic module. Let $W_\mu$ be the $R$-span of the $m_{st}$ with $s$ $\mu$-flagged. Right multiplication by a finite generator $T_i$ uses the Murphy expansion of [F3]: same-shape terms retain the left tableau, and higher terms arise from ordinary straightening inside physical components whose permutations are products of $d(s)$ with permutations internal to the physical intervals, hence only permute the admissible $\mu$-labels among the nodes of each component; the exact quadratic expansion, row normalization, and straightening inside components preserve the flagged set. Right multiplication by $X_1$ keeps the same-shape term and, in the higher component-shift term of the proved formula, moves one node of physical component $k$ to component $k-1$ with its $\mu$-component label unchanged: in cumulative-profile form the boundary $A_{k-1}$ increases by one and no other boundary decreases, so every previously valid rank rectangle of step 1.2 stays valid, and sorting and subsequent finite straightening happen inside the new component intervals; the $k=1$ term vanishes. The algebra is generated by the $T_i$ and $X_1$, and $X_1^{-1}$ is a polynomial in $X_1$ by the cyclotomic relation, so this proves that $W_\mu$ is a right ideal; since $m_\mu\in W_\mu$ (its initial tableau has equal physical and type components) we get $M_\mu\subseteq W_\mu$. The same support tracking for left generators inside one $\mu$-row keeps the flag, so $W_\mu$ and its cellular-ideal filtration are left modules for the $\mu$-row parabolic, and $m_\mu=x_\mu u_\mu$ makes every $m\in M_\mu$ satisfy $T_im=zm$ for $\mu$-row generators. [F1, F3, algebra]

Exact unlocalized membership. Expand $b_0u_\lambda$ in the left affine PBW basis $X^aT_w$ of [F2]; its coefficients lie in $P=R^{\mathrm{univ}}[X_1^{\pm1},\dots,X_n^{\pm1}]$. Membership in $u_\mu H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}[(X_i-X_j)^{-1}]$ from step 2.1 says each coefficient lies in $u_\mu P[(X_i-X_j)^{-1}]$. Every factor $X_j-U_k$ of $u_\mu$ is a prime of the unique factorization domain $P$, is not associated to any difference $X_i-X_j$, and is not inverted by the localization, so its multiplicity cannot drop when passing to the localization; hence each coefficient is already divisible by $u_\mu$ in $P$. Therefore the PBW coordinates of $u_\mu^{-1}b_0u_\lambda$ are actual Laurent polynomials and there is an exact unlocalized equality $b_0u_\lambda=u_\mu b$ with $b\in H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Eigenvalue descent and the explicit element $h$. Let $i$ be a generator of the $\mu$-row subgroup, so that $i,i+1$ lie in one $\mu$-component interval. Expand the double coset into disjoint left cosets, choosing the minimal representative $r$ of each coset. Length additivity gives $b_0=\sum_r x_\mu T_r$, so $T_ib_0=zb_0$ by pairing the row-subgroup words under left multiplication by $s_i$; right multiplication by $u_\lambda$ retains this left eigenvalue, so $T_i(u_\mu b)=zu_\mu b$. The element $u_\mu$ is symmetric in the variables of each $\mu$-interval, so it commutes with $T_i$, and injectivity of left multiplication by the nonzero Laurent polynomial $u_\mu$ ([F2]) cancels it, giving $T_ib=zb$. Write $b=\sum_wT_wf_w$ in the right PBW basis ([F2]). For each $w$ with $\ell(s_iw)=\ell(w)+1$, comparing coefficients of $T_{s_iw}$ in $T_ib=zb$ gives $f_w+(z-1)f_{s_iw}=zf_{s_iw}$ by the quadratic relation $(T_i-z)(T_i+1)=0$, hence $f_w=f_{s_iw}$; thus $f$ is constant on each left coset $S_\mu w$. Taking minimal-length coset representatives $r$ and using the length-additive expansion $x_\mu T_r=\sum_{\sigma\in S_\mu}T_{\sigma r}$ gives $b=x_\mu h_0$ with $h_0=\sum_rT_rf_r\in H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$. Since $x_\mu$ commutes with $u_\mu$, the explicit sum defining $m_{(S,t)}$ becomes $m_{(S,t)}=b_0u_\lambda T_{d(t)}=u_\mu x_\mu h_0T_{d(t)}=m_\mu h$ with $h=h_0T_{d(t)}$; this constructs $h$ by finite coset enumeration and polynomial division with no inverted quantum factorial, and the equality is exact, so the Murphy coefficient at the pivot $m_{s_0t}$ is $1$. [F1, F2, step 3.1, algebra]

Generic upper bound by the finite Mackey count. Over the field $K$ of fractions of the universal Laurent ring, the finite type-A Hecke algebra and each row parabolic are split semisimple with simple ordinary Specht modules and trivial-character multiplicities equal to the ordinary semistandard numbers ([F4], whose generic-multiplicity step uses the cellular-head theory [F7] and the content separation of [F8]); the finite $T_w$ basis and multiplication rule [F5] realize the double-coset decompositions below by explicit basis maps. Restricting the shape-$\lambda$ left cell module to the $\mu$-row parabolic and applying the finite double-coset decomposition splits it as the direct sum over the allocation matrices $N=(N_{r,b})$ recording how many entries of $\mu$-row $r$ enter physical component $b$; the trivial-character multiplicity is $\sum_{N\ \text{flag-compatible}}\prod_bK_{(\lambda^{(b)},\rho_b)}$, which is in bijection with $\#\operatorname{SStd}_\mu(\lambda)$ by reading off each component's ordinary semistandard tableau. By the cellular-ideal filtration [F3] the $\lambda$-layer of $W_\mu$ is the flagged left cell tensored with the full right cell, so exactness of the trivial-character multiplicity gives $\dim_K(W_\mu)^{\mathrm{triv}}=\sum_\lambda\#\operatorname{SStd}_\mu(\lambda)\#\operatorname{Std}_\lambda$. By step 2.2, $M_\mu^K\subseteq(W_\mu)^{\mathrm{triv}}$, while step 4.1 puts all $\sum_\lambda\#\operatorname{SStd}_\mu(\lambda)\#\operatorname{Std}_\lambda$ sums $m_{(S,t)}$ inside $M_\mu^K$ and their disjoint coefficient-$1$ Murphy fibres make them independent; the two bounds agree, so $M_\mu^K$ is exactly their $K$-span. [F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, step 4.1, step 2.2, algebra]

Assign to each standard multitableau the sequence of joint Jucys–Murphy words: the diagonal values $U_az^{j-i}$ at the nodes carrying the labels $1,\dots,n$ ([F3]). If two standard multitableaux first differ at step $r$, then their restrictions to the boxes $1,\dots,r-1$ coincide, and the two added nodes are two different addable nodes of that common prefix shape. If the two nodes lie in one physical component, their contents $j-i$ are different (two addable nodes of a partition have different contents), and $z$ is transcendental over the base field, so $z^{j-i}\ne z^{j'-i'}$. If they lie in different components $a\ne b$, the values $U_az^{j-i}$ and $U_bz^{j'-i'}$ are distinct in $K$, because $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$ are algebraically independent monomials and the components differ. Hence the joint word determines the tableau, different standard multitableaux -- even of different shapes -- have different joint words, and distinct shapes have disjoint sets of word characters. Generic simplicity and split semisimplicity. By [F3] each $S_\lambda$ has a simultaneous triangular filtration whose successive characters are its own words of step 1.1. Hence every composition factor $D_\mu$ of the nonzero module $S_\lambda$ has a word occurring in $S_\mu$ and a word occurring in $S_\lambda$; disjointness of shape word sets forces $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $D_\lambda\ne0$, and the cellular diagonal multiplicity $[S_\lambda:D_\lambda]=1$ of [F4] forces $S_\lambda=D_\lambda$ to be simple, with the distinct absolutely simple modules $S_\lambda$ as the only composition factors. The cellular basis gives $\dim_K H_K=\sum_\lambda(\dim_K S_\lambda)^2$. The semisimple quotient is a product of full matrix algebras on the exhaustive absolutely simple $S_\lambda$: to see this, the rank-one cell action on each simple gives every matrix unit, and the distinct simple labels give the distinct simple factors. Its dimension is the same sum, so the radical has dimension zero. Thus $H_K$ is split semisimple; no splitting of the cellular filtration was assumed. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

For two standard multitableaux that first differ at a step $r\le N$, the common prefix of size $r-1$ has components of sizes summing to $r-1$; the two added nodes lie in components $a,b$ and each added content $c=j-i$ is bounded in absolute value by the size of its own component, so $|c-c'|<r\le N$. A collision $U_az^c=U_bz^{c'}$ with $a\ne b$ would force the equality $Na+c=Nb+c'$ of $t$-adic exponents, i.e. the nonzero multiple $N(a-b)$ of $N$ would equal $c'-c$ with $|c'-c|<N$, impossible. If $a=b$, then $z$ is transcendental over $F$, so $z^c=z^{c'}$ forces $c=c'$. citations.quote: Work with the arbitrary-level Murphy/Schur datum of [[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]] over either (i) the fraction field $K$ of the universal Laurent parameter ring, including the generic field of the Lyle–Mathas deformation, or (ii) any field $F$ with nonzero $q_H,Q_1,\dots,Q_\ell$ under the deformation $z=q_Ht$, $U_a=Q_at^{na}$ in $F(t)$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $F[t,t^{-1}]$ be its Laurent polynomial ring ([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]), and let $v_1$ be the $(t-1)$-adic valuation on the nonzero elements of $F[t,t^{-1}]$: for $0\ne f$, $$v_1(f):=\max\{n\ge0:(t-1)^n\mid f\ \text{in}\ F[t,t^{-1}]\},$$ so that $v_1(f)=0$ exactly when $f(1)\ne0$ ([[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]).
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge0$ and $\ell\ge1$, and let $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$ be units of $R$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $[\lambda]$ be its Young diagram ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A **tableau of shape $\lambda$**, or $\lambda$-tableau, is a bijection $$t:[\lambda]\longrightarrow\{1,2,\dots,n\}.$$ We write $t(i,j)$ for the entry of $t$ in the node $(i,j)$, and we display $t$ as the diagram $[\lambda]$ with each node carrying its entry.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$, with diagrams $[\lambda]$ and $[\mu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For content counts only, set $\mu_i:=0$ for $i$ beyond the number of parts of $\mu$; these zeros are not additional parts of the partition.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is $$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$ The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

derivations.claim: Characters as finite symmetric polynomials. Fix $d\ge n$ row labels per type component with ordered variables $x_{(a,r)}$, put $Y_a=\{x_{(b,r)}:b\ge a\}$ with the inherited order, and for a shape $\lambda$ let $\operatorname{ch}_\lambda(x)=\sum_{T\in\operatorname{SStd}(\lambda)}x^{\operatorname{wt}(T)}$. The flag condition says that the physical component $a$ of a semistandard tableau is an ordinary semistandard tableau over the alphabet $Y_a$, and the components are chosen independently, so $\operatorname{ch}_\lambda(x)=\prod_a s_{\lambda^{(a)}}(Y_a)$ with $s_\rho(Y)=\det(h_{\rho_i-i+j}(Y))$. The determinant equals the ordinary semistandard generating polynomial: expand it as signed families of east/north lattice paths from $(-j,1)$ to $(\rho_i-i,m)$ with east steps at height $r$ weighted $y_r$, choose the first intersection in a fixed order and exchange the two tails, an involution that preserves the monomial weight and reverses the permutation sign, so all intersecting families cancel; a nonintersecting family forces the identity matching, and the surviving families are exactly the semistandard tableaux, sign $+1$. Hence the coefficient of $x^\nu$ in $\operatorname{ch}_\lambda$ is the Kostka number $K_{\lambda\nu}$; empty and short-row cases are included. [F3, F4, F5, algebra]

Beta determinants and rim-hook signs. Choose $N\ge n$, put $\beta_{a,i}=\lambda^{(a)}_i+N-i$ with zero parts appended, and for a nonnegative integer array $v$ define $\chi(v;x)=\prod_a\det\bigl(h_{v_{a,i}-N+j}(Y_a)\bigr)_{i,j}$. If two entries of one component of $v$ agree the determinant has equal rows and is zero; otherwise sorting that component into strictly decreasing order and writing $\rho_i=v'_i-N+i$ gives $\chi(v;x)=\varepsilon(v)\prod_a s_{\rho^{(a)}}(Y_a)$ with $\varepsilon$ the product of the row-sorting signs, so every coefficient is a signed Kostka multiplicity. A beta move lowering a bead from $v+L$ to an unoccupied $v$ is exactly the removal of a rim hook of length $L$: tracing the southeast boundary shows the strip between the two boundary steps has $L$ boxes, its leg is the number of occupied positions strictly between $v$ and $v+L$, its foot content is $v-N+1$, and the associated sorting sign is $(-1)^{\operatorname{leg}}$; the correspondence is a bijection by the reverse move. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

The hook side as a complete finite alternating polynomial. Define $B_\lambda(x)$ as the finite alternating sum of step 2.1: for crosscomponent terms, over $a<b$, over beads $i,j$ and lengths $h\le\beta_{a,i}$, of $\chi(\beta-h e_{a,i}+h e_{b,j};x)V(U_az^{\beta_{a,i}-h}-U_bz^{\beta_{b,j}})$; and for same-component terms, over $a$, $i<j$ and $1\le h\le\beta_{a,i}-\beta_{a,j}-1$, of $\chi(\beta-he_{a,i}+he_{a,j};x)V(U_az^{\beta_{a,i}-h}-U_az^{\beta_{a,j}})$; terms whose $\chi$ is the zero polynomial are omitted before any valuation is evaluated. Then $B_\lambda(x)=\sum_{\mu:\lambda\triangleright\mu}J_{\lambda\mu}\operatorname{ch}_\mu(x)$: a crosscomponent move removing from the earlier component $a$ and adding to a later component $b>a$ produces a strictly dominated $\mu$ and occurs exactly once by the bead description; occupied targets give repeated rows and zero; sorting contributes $(-1)^{\text{removed leg}+\text{added leg}}$; and the prefactor $z^{-N+1}$ converts the beta difference to the difference of the deformed foot residues. In one component the two moved beads $i<j$ give a strict dominance decrease precisely for $1\le h<\beta_i-\beta_j$, the exchange case $h=\beta_i-\beta_j$ giving $\mu=\lambda$ and the outward case giving the reverse dominance; occupied intermediate positions again give zero rows, and the range exceeding a component's size gives a repeated or negative bead, hence a zero determinant. Thus no hook pair is lost or added, and the surviving summands are exactly the $J_{\lambda\mu}$ terms. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

Nonvanishing of every retained foot difference. For a removable rim hook of length $L$ from a partition of size $M+L$ with foot $(h,j)$, one has $-(M+L-1)\le j-h\le M$: every box left of the foot in its row survives, so $j-1\le M$, and $h\le M+L$ gives the lower bound. If $\lambda$ and $\mu$ remove equal-length hooks in distinct components $a\ne b$ to the same remainder with remainder sizes $M_a,M_b$, their foot contents satisfy $|\gamma_x-\gamma_y|\le M_a+M_b+L-1\le n-1$, so the exponent $n(a-b)+\gamma_x-\gamma_y$ is a nonzero integer; in the same component equal foot content and equal length reconstruct the same inverse hook addition, hence would force $\lambda=\mu$, which the strict-dominance terms exclude. Therefore every retained Laurent difference $U_az^u-U_bz^v$ is nonzero in $F(t)$: it is a unit times a nonzero Laurent monomial times $(z^{N}-1)$-type factors and, by [F2], its valuation is finite, being $0$ when the constant residues differ, $1$ in characteristic zero when they agree, and $p^{v_p(N)}$ in characteristic $p$ when they agree. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

The same-component operator. In the same-component beta sum put $D=\beta_i-\beta_j$ and $k=D-h$, so the valuation is $f(k)=V(z^k-1)$ up to unit factors; swapping the two changed determinant rows shows $\chi(\beta-(D-k)e_i+(D-k)e_j;x)=-\chi(\beta-ke_i+ke_j;x)$. Hence the complete coefficient of $f(k)$ is $-\sum_{i<j:\beta_i-\beta_j>k}\chi(\beta-ke_i+ke_j;x)$, which is the strictly dominance-lowering part of $-p_kp_k^\perp$ on the abstract shape basis, where $p_k^\perp$ lowers an occupied bead by $k$ into an unoccupied nonnegative position with sign $(-1)^{\#\text{crossed beads}}$ and $p_k$ raises a bead by $k$ with the same sign rule; the bead-raising formula follows from the alternant identity $\det(y_r^{\beta_i})\sum_ry_r^k=\sum_i\det(y_r^{\beta_i+k\delta_{ij}})$ divided by the Vandermonde, and the removal map is its transpose. After one removal and one addition a non-diagonal lower-dominance result comes only from distinct beads $i<j$ with $0<k<\beta_i-\beta_j$, occupied intermediate positions giving zero repeated rows and the diagonal being removed by the strict projection; this proves the operator identification integrally, in every characteristic. [step 2.1, algebra]

The crosscomponent operator as exterior currents. On the $N$-fold exterior power of a space with basis $e_0,e_1,\dots$, represent a partition by the ordered wedge of its beta beads and let $E(p,q)$ insert $e_p$ after removing $e_q$, with exterior signs; it vanishes if $q$ is absent or $p$ is occupied, and its sign is the bead-sorting sign. Expanding $E=\text{creation}\cdot\text{contraction}$ gives $[E(p,q),E(r,s)]=\delta_{q,r}E(p,s)-\delta_{p,s}E(r,q)$. The crosscomponent matrix acting on column shape vectors is $J^{\mathrm{cross}}=\sum_{a<b}\sum_{h>0}\sum_{q\ge h,w\ge0}V(U_az^{q-h}-U_bz^w)E_a(q,q-h)E_b(w,w+h)$, a finite operator on each size-$n$ sector; the reverse hook pair has forward current $E_a(q-h,q)E_b(w+h,w)$, and transposing gives exactly this operator with the same signs and valuation. [step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, algebra]

Horizontal strips and their conjugation. With $S e_q=e_{q+1}$ and $H(x)=(I-xS)^{-1}=\sum_{r\ge0}x^rS^r$, whose entry $H_{p,q}$ is $x^{p-q}$ for $p\ge q$ and $0$ otherwise, the matrix of $\wedge^NH(x)$ between $\beta_\mu$ and $\beta_\rho$ is $x^{|\mu|-|\rho|}\det(1_{\beta_{\mu,i}\ge\beta_{\rho,j}})$. Subtracting consecutive columns of the $0/1$ matrix makes its determinant $1$ exactly when $\beta_{\mu,i}\ge\beta_{\rho,i}>\beta_{\mu,i+1}$ for all $i$, i.e. $\mu_i\ge\rho_i\ge\mu_{i+1}$, the horizontal-strip criterion, and $0$ otherwise; so $\Gamma(x)=\wedge^NH(x)$ adds every horizontal strip once with weight $x^{\text{strip size}}$. For a type component $a$, $\Gamma_a(x)=\prod_{b\le a}\Gamma_b(x)$ adds a horizontal strip in every permitted physical component $b\le a$ and leaves the rest unchanged, so the successive $\Gamma_a$ from the empty shape enumerate exactly the flagged semistandard tableaux and give the branching matrix. Conjugation is explicit: since $H^{-1}=I-xS$ has column vector $e_p-xe_{p+1}$ and row covector $\sum_{r\le q}x^{q-r}e_r^*$, $\Gamma(x)^{-1}E(p,q)\Gamma(x)=\sum_{r=0}^qx^{q-r}\bigl(E(p,r)-xE(p+1,r)\bigr),$ and the two-current conjugation is the ordered product of two such sums. [step 4.1, algebra]

The marked-strip factor and the local commutator identity. For a permitted $\Gamma_a$ transition $\rho\to\lambda$ with new-node set $\eta$, put $r_x=U_{\operatorname{comp}(x)}z^{\operatorname{content}(x)}$ and $F^{(a)}_{\lambda\rho}=\prod_{x\in\eta}\prod_{\operatorname{comp}(x)<b\le a}(r_x-U_b)\prod_{\substack{x\in[\rho],\,y\in\eta\\x,y\ \text{same physical row}}}C_+(r_x,r_y)\prod_{\substack{x<y,\ x,y\in\eta\\\text{different physical rows}}}C_+(r_x,r_y)\prod_{\substack{x\in\eta,\,y\in[\rho]\\x<y}}R(r_x,r_y).$ Splitting the node pairs of [F1] into old/old, old/new and new/new pairs shows that along any semistandard chain the product of these factors is exactly $\gamma_{t_T}/(C_{t_T}u_T)$; older labels are smaller than the new label, same-row old/new pairs and same-label new/new pairs give $C_+$, a row-reading-earlier new node before an old node is a different-label inversion giving $R$, and all other pairs give nothing. Then $(J_n\Gamma_a^{(n,m)}-\Gamma_a^{(n,m)}J_m)_{\lambda\rho}=x^{n-m}V(F^{(a)}_{\lambda\rho})$ on permitted transitions and $0$ otherwise, on the reachable prefix sector. On support this is the exact row/column minor computation: the strip matrix is upper unitriangular, the row- and column-replacement determinants are $d_i^{\mathrm{row}}(v)=1_{p_i\le v<p_{i-1}}$ and $d_i^{\mathrm{col}}(v)=1_{q_{i+1}<v\le q_i}$ with $p_0=\infty$, the $J\Gamma$ term of index $j+1$ pairs with the $\Gamma J$ term of index $j$ sharing the bound $K_j=p_{b,j}-q_{b,j+1}-1$, and the elementary interval identity $\sum_{s=0}^{M-1}(\psi(A+s+K+1)-\psi(A+s+1))=\sum_{h=1}^{\min(M,K)}(\psi(A+M+K+1-h)-\psi(A+h))$ matches the two sides term by term, with $\psi(d)=V(U_az^d-U_b)$; the same-component telescoping is the analogue of this computation with the boundary factor. Off support, the defective strip step matrix has rank at most $N-2$, whence both sides vanish, or rank $N-1$ with one missing tail type $[P,P')$ and one duplicated type $(Q',Q]$; then the adjugate is $\varepsilon vu^{\mathsf T}$ with $u=e_i-e_{i+1}$, $v=e_r-e_{r-1}$ and one common sign, and replacing a row or column at position $x$ gives $D_{\mathrm{row}}(x)=\varepsilon u_l1_{P\le x<P'}$ and $D_{\mathrm{col}}(x)=\varepsilon v_l1_{Q'<x\le Q}$, so the a-only, b-only and both-defective cases cancel by the displayed interval translations; in the deficiency-two pattern with duplicate thresholds $r<s$ and missing intervals $I_1,I_2$ strictly between them, the row-side coefficient of $\phi(k)$ is $\varepsilon(A_{I_1}(k)B_{I_2}(k)-A_{I_2}(k)B_{I_1}(k))$ and the column-side coefficient is the same expression after the endpoint-reciprocity substitution $A_{I}=D^-$, $B_{I}=D^+$, so every formal coefficient cancels exactly, including adjacent missing thresholds and overlapping column groups, and higher deficiency kills both sides. [F1, F6, step 3.3, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

Telescoping and the valuation formula. Multiply the $\Gamma$ matrices in increasing type-row-label order and telescope $J\Gamma-\Gamma J$ from $J_0=0$; by step 6.1 each commutator inserts exactly $V(F)$ at its strip position, so the $\lambda$-coordinate of the resulting identity is $\sum_T V(\gamma_{t_T}/(C_{t_T}u_T))x^{\operatorname{wt}(T)}=L_\lambda(x)$ on one side and $B_\lambda(x)$ on the other. All padded artificial symbols cancel before the surviving coefficients are evaluated, and every surviving coefficient corresponds to a valid current, hence by step 3.2 to a nonzero foot difference with finite valuation. Comparing with the exact monic product [F1] and the hook side of step 3.1, and taking the coefficient of $x^
u$ at an actual multipartition weight $
u$ (auxiliary compositions only index the same polynomials and never enter the Schur conclusion), gives $V(\det G_{\lambda
u})=\sum_\mu J_{\lambda\mu}K_{\mu
u};$ the empty case $n=0$ gives $0$, all ranks keep the fixed parameters $z=q_Ht$, $U_a=Q_at^{na}$, and arbitrary-composition coefficients are combinatorial only. [F1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. 2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit

form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism

derivations.claim: One component at a time, at level one. Suppose first that the component sizes agree. For a single component $a$ of rank $m$, the actual level-one Hecke algebra is the finite Hecke algebra by [F3]. Its same-core Specht-block clause [F4], together with the level-one case of the Jantzen linkage equivalence [F1], connects any two rank-$m$ partitions with equal $e$-core by level-one Jantzen edges. The Dipper–James to Murphy convention change is conjugate-dual, and core equality is preserved because the core of the transpose is the transpose of the core, so the exact existing clause applies over the original field $F$ without an algebraic-closure hypothesis. The rank $m=0$ case has a single empty partition and needs no block theorem. [F1, F3, F4, F5]

Equalizing the component weights. If the component weights differ, choose a component whose weight exceeds its target and one whose weight is deficient; a positive-weight component has a removable $e$-hook by its core construction [F5]. For any prescribed foot residue $f$, moving the lowest bead on runner $f-1$ down by $e$ creates an $e$-hook with that foot residue, since its foot residue is the starting beta position plus one; wrap this hook in the deficient component with the same foot residue. The changed components determine the removed and added hook pair uniquely, and in the appropriate dominance orientation their $J$ contribution is one signed valuation with no cancellation; equal foot residues mean the nonzero generic difference is divisible by $t-1$, so the valuation is a positive integer. Nonzero generic foot differences are part of the exact formula [F2], and no unit-difference or characteristic-zero restriction is inserted. Thus the transfer is a Jantzen edge; it lowers the sum of squares of the discrepancies of the component hook weights by at least $2$, so finitely many such transfers equalize the component weights. Every moved $e$-hook preserves its component's core by [F5], and every step preserves the total rank. [F2, F5]

Fixed component sizes. For two full multipartitions that differ only in component $a$, every contributing equal-remainder hook pair in $J$ lies in $a$: the other components are unchanged on both sides and cancelling hooks between two unchanged components would return the same multipartition. The common residue factor $Q_at^{na}$ is a unit of $\mathcal O$, and replacing it by the level-one factor $Q_at^m$ multiplies each foot difference by a Laurent unit, so the valuation is unchanged and the full-level $J$ coefficient equals the level-one coefficient of [F2]. Inserting the level-one paths of step 1.1 in component $a$ and leaving the other components fixed connects all multipartitions with equal component sizes and the same component cores. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

Conclusion. Steps 1.2 equalize component sizes along Jantzen edges from any starting multipartition, and step 2.1 connects all multipartitions of fixed component sizes with equal component cores. Composing the two finite chains connects any two multipartitions of rank $n$ with equal componentwise $e$-cores, proving that they are $J$-equivalent; the fixed-size comparison of coefficients is step 2.1. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 1.2] ∎

derivations.claim: Base cases. At rank $0$ the algebra is $F$, the empty-word projector is $1$, and this is its unique primitive central idempotent. At positive rank and level $0$ the defining polynomial is $1$, so the algebra is $0$ and every content sector is $0$, with no nonzero blocks. Hence assume rank $d\ge1$ and level $\ell\ge1$. [F1]

The degenerate branch. In the branch $q_H=1$ necessarily $\operatorname{char}F=e>0$. The center is the full symmetric-polynomial image over this $F$ by [F3], and [F4] applies to the early CRT projectors and proves that their content sums are zero or primitive. This uses neither a field extension nor a power-sum generation assertion. [F1, F3, F4]

The nondegenerate branch: labels of sectors. In the branch $q_H\ne1$ choose a charge list $c_1,\dots,c_\ell$ repeating each $i$ exactly $\lambda_i$ times, so $Q_a=q_H^{c_a}$ and the first polynomial is unchanged. The arbitrary-level Murphy cellular basis and the finite cellular head lemma [F5] supply all simple $H_d^\Lambda$-modules as nonzero Specht quotients $D^\lambda$, and the content-triangular JM action [F6] says every word on $S^\lambda$, hence on $D^\lambda$, has the node content $C(\lambda)$. Thus a simple module lying in a nonzero sector $e_\alpha$ has a label $\lambda$ with $C(\lambda)=\alpha$. [F1, F5, F6]

Primitivity of the nonzero sectors. Any two simple modules in the sector $e_\alpha$ have labels with equal content, so [F7] connects the labels by integer Jantzen edges and [F8] transfers this to a common Hecke block. If $e_\alpha$ decomposed into two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents $u,v$, the nonzero finite algebras $uH_d^\Lambda$ and $vH_d^\Lambda$ would each have a simple module, obtained from a proper right ideal of maximal dimension. Those simple modules cannot lie in one block, because the central idempotent $u$ acts as the identity on the first and as zero on the second, and all modules and extensions split by $u$. This contradicts the one-block assertion, so $e_\alpha$ is primitive. [F1, F7, F8, step 1.3]

Every block is a content sector. In either branch let $b$ be a primitive central idempotent and write $b=\sum_\alpha be_\alpha$. The terms are central orthogonal idempotents, so precisely one is nonzero and $b=be_\alpha$; primitivity of the nonzero $e_\alpha$ from step 1.2 or step 2.1 gives $b=e_\alpha$. Hence the nonzero content sums are exactly all primitive central idempotents and the decomposition $H_d^\Lambda=\bigoplus_\alpha e_\alpha H_d^\Lambda$ is precisely the block decomposition [F2]. All sums are finite, the field characteristic never reduces an integer $K_0$ adjacency, and no affine-block classification or citation-only center theorem is consumed. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎
